title: From one producer to the market

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Build market supply by adding the supplies of individual producers together, price by price.

blocks.heading: One seller, then all of them
blocks.text: Individual supply is the quantity of a good that one producer is willing and able to offer for sale at each price. Market supply is the quantity that all the producers in a market together are willing and able to offer at that price. Bread in Katutura comes from many small bakeries: one bakery's daily offering is individual supply; the loaves all Katutura's bakeries offer together make up the market's supply.

blocks.heading: Adding the schedules
blocks.text: Oshakati Textiles weaves cloth for the northern market. At N$25 a metre it offers 400 metres a week. A second weaver offers 600 metres a week at the same price, and every other producer together offers 1 500 metres. Market supply at N$25 is found by adding across producers at that price: 400 + 600 = 1 000 metres, and 1 000 + 1 500 = 2 500 metres a week. The same addition is done at each other price, and the market supply curve is the horizontal sum of the individual curves. A weaving firm in Kyoto in Japan books its metres into its own market's total the same way.

blocks.heading: Why adding is the whole method
blocks.text: Market supply counts what every seller in the market offers at a price, so the market figure at each price is the sum of the individual figures at that same price. Adding price by price matters: adding one producer's quantities across different prices answers a different question. A new firm entering the market adds its offering at each price, so the market supply curve tends to sit further right than before.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Topic 2.3 built market demand by adding individual buyers; this topic does the same for sellers, and topic 2.5 needs both totals to set the price.
